deferred.name: Conformal block coefficients are squared real OPE coefficients
deferred.statement: For a normalized real scalar in a unitary conformal field theory, the reduced four-point correlation function has the convergent expansion $g(u,v)=\sum_O f_{\phi\phi O}^2 g_{\Delta_O,\ell_O}(u,v)$. Each coefficient is nonnegative, and only even symmetric traceless spins occur.
hypotheses: The scalar is real and identical in all four insertions, and the primary basis is real and orthonormal. The Euclidean dimension is at least 2, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.

The theory is unitary and the two pairs admit a separating radial sphere. The normalizable pair states have a complete orthogonal conformal-family decomposition, and rotations include O(d) reflections.

steps.text: For each primary multiplet, form its orthogonal projector using an orthonormal descendant basis. Completeness makes the identity equal to the sum of these projectors, with null states removed. The overlap of a descendant with the scalar pair is a derivative of the primary three-point function, by the conformal Ward identity. So a family whose primary has zero scalar-scalar coupling gives zero for all its descendants. A scalar pair on an axis is invariant under its O(d-1) stabilizer. The primary overlap, as a function on the sphere, is a spherical harmonic. Its tensor representatives are symmetric traceless tensors. Thus only primaries with these spin representations have a nonzero scalar-pair overlap, and all other families drop out.

Fix a multiplet $O$. The state of the first pair, projected on $O$, has the primary overlap $f_{\phi\phi O}$. This is a coupling to the ket $|O\rangle$. The second pair is the image of a first-type pair under inversion in the separating sphere. Radial adjoints give $P_\mu^*=K_\mu$, so the bra of a pair is the conjugate of the ket of its inverted pair. Hence its overlap with $\langle O|$ is the complex conjugate of the ket coupling at the inverted points. The coupling is real, so the conjugate has the same value $f_{\phi\phi O}$. The inversion acts on the spin-$\ell$ tensor structure by an orthogonal reflection. This gives a factor $(-1)^\ell$ at most. The second coupling is therefore $(-1)^\ell f_{\phi\phi O}$. The exchange of one multiplet then has the conformal block as its position dependence. The couplings multiply to $(-1)^\ell f_{\phi\phi O}^2$. Step s3 shows that only even $\ell$ remain. For these the product is $f_{\phi\phi O}^2$.

The scalar-scalar-spin numerator changes by $(-1)^\ell$ under exchange of the equal scalars. Hence odd-spin couplings vanish. Every remaining real coefficient has nonnegative square. Pairing the convergent projector sum gives the full expansion.

applications.title: Inspect coefficients in a trial bootstrap expansion
applications.inputs: Suppose a normalized real scalar has candidate exchange couplings $f_1=1$, $f_2=-2$, and $f_3=1/2$.
applications.hypotheses: All three exchanges lie in even-spin multiplets of a unitary theory.

steps.text: The expansion coefficients are $1^2=1$, $(-2)^2=4$, and $(1/2)^2=1/4$.
A negative coupling can occur, but it contributes a positive square to this identical-scalar correlator.

applications.conclusion: The proposed block weights are $1,4,1/4$, and none is negative.

limitations: This is a result within the explicitly stated conformal field theory framework, not an existence theorem for an interacting model.

deferred.name: Conformal blocks satisfy the quadratic Casimir equation
deferred.statement: For identical external scalars in a conformal field theory, an exchanged spin-$\ell$ primary of dimension $\Delta$ gives a block with correlation function eigenvalue $\mathcal Dg_{\Delta,\ell}=[\Delta(\Delta-d)+\ell(\ell+d-2)]g_{\Delta,\ell}$. Here $\mathcal D$ is the differential Casimir of the first pair after removal of its scalar prefactor.
hypotheses: The exchanged conformal multiplet is generated by a primary of dimension $\Delta$ and symmetric traceless spin $\ell$. The Euclidean dimension is at least 2, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.
The external fields are identical scalar primaries, and the four positions are separated. The radial theory is unitary and admits the orthogonal conformal-family projectors of its block expansion.

steps.text: Write the Casimir in dilation, translation, special conformal, and rotation generators. The primary conditions $K|O\rangle=0$ and $D|O\rangle=\Delta|O\rangle$ reduce its eigenvalue to $\Delta(\Delta-d)+\ell(\ell+d-2)$. Centrality gives the same value on descendants.

The projector onto an irreducible multiplet commutes with conformal generators. Acting with the Casimir on the state from the first scalar pair is therefore equivalent to its eigenvalue acting on the projected exchange.

Each conformal generator acts on the two external scalar positions by its primary differential operator. Sum the two actions, square to form the pair Casimir, then remove the usual four-point prefactor. The resulting operator $\mathcal D$ acts only on $u,v$ and has the stated eigenvalue on the block.

applications.title: Find the Casimir eigenvalue of stress-tensor exchange
applications.hypotheses: The stress tensor is an exchanged symmetric traceless conformal primary.

steps.text: The dilation part is $3(3-3)=0$.
The rotation part is $2(2+3-2)=6$. Thus the block solves $\mathcal Dg=6g$.

applications.conclusion: The stress-tensor block has quadratic Casimir eigenvalue 6.

deferred.name: Hypergeometric global conformal blocks in two dimensions
deferred.statement: For identical scalar insertions in a two-dimensional conformal field theory, the symmetrized global block is $k_{\Delta+\ell}(z)k_{\Delta-\ell}(\bar z)+k_{\Delta-\ell}(z)k_{\Delta+\ell}(\bar z)$, where $k_\beta(t)=t^{\beta/2}\,{}_2F_1(\beta/2,\beta/2;\beta;t)$. Its normalization is the symmetrized one of the cited correlation function formula.
hypotheses: Only the global conformal algebra is used, and the external operators are identical scalars. The spacetime dimension is exactly 2, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.

The parameters avoid hypergeometric poles and the block has the primary OPE asymptotics on the chosen analytic branch. After extraction of each primary power, the residual function is analytic at zero and has value 1 there. The theory is unitary, and the block is the contribution of one conformal family through an orthogonal projector, as the cited Casimir theorem requires.

steps.text: In two dimensions, the conformal algebra splits into two commuting copies of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. The generators are $L_{-1},L_0,L_1$ and $\bar L_{-1},\bar L_0,\bar L_1$. The holomorphic Casimir is $C_h=L_0^2-\tfrac12(L_1L_{-1}+L_{-1}L_1)$. $C_{\bar h}$ is the same expression in the barred generators. On a primary, $L_1|O\rangle=0$, $L_0|O\rangle=h|O\rangle$ and $[L_1,L_{-1}]=2L_0$. So $C_h|O\rangle=(h^2-h)|O\rangle=h(h-1)|O\rangle$. In the same way $C_{\bar h}|O\rangle=\bar h(\bar h-1)|O\rangle$. Here $h=(\Delta+\ell)/2$ and $\bar h=(\Delta-\ell)/2$. Each Casimir commutes with both copies, so it has the same value on every descendant and commutes with the projector onto the family. The cited pair Casimir is $2(C_h+C_{\bar h})$. Check: $2[h(h-1)+\bar h(\bar h-1)]=\Delta(\Delta-2)+\ell^2$, which is the cited eigenvalue for $d=2$. On the two external points, $C_h$ acts as a differential operator in $z$ only, and $C_{\bar h}$ in $\bar z$ only. So the block $G$ obeys $D_zG=h(h-1)G$ and $D_{\bar z}G=\bar h(\bar h-1)G$ separately, with $D_t=t^2(1-t)\partial_t^2-t^2\partial_t$. Each equation has a two-dimensional solution space in its own variable. So $G$ is a sum of products of one-variable solutions. The primary powers and the branch in the hypotheses keep one product, which s2 finds.
The equation $[t^2(1-t)\partial_t^2-t^2\partial_t]k_{2h}=h(h-1)k_{2h}$ becomes the hypergeometric equation after $k_{2h}=t^hF(t)$. The solution analytic at zero with $F(0)=1$ is ${}_2F_1(h,h;2h;t)$.

Multiply the holomorphic solution by the antiholomorphic solution, then add the term with $h,\bar h$ exchanged. This gives the stated symmetrized normalization. At spin zero the formula contains two identical terms. Divide by 2 if a unit leading scalar block is desired; it is not a Virasoro block.

applications.title: Evaluate a simple holomorphic factor without a series
applications.hypotheses: Use $0<t<1$, away from the hypergeometric branch cut.

steps.text: Integrating the geometric series gives ${}_2F_1(1,1;2;t)=-\log(1-t)/t$.
Thus $k_2(1/2)=\log2$. For a spin-zero dimension-2 symmetrized global block at $z=\bar z=1/2$, the value is $2(\log2)^2$.

applications.conclusion: The symmetrized global block evaluates to $2(\log2)^2$.

limitations: This is a result within the explicitly stated conformal field theory framework, not an existence theorem for an interacting model.

deferred.name: Dolan-Osborn hypergeometric conformal blocks in four dimensions
deferred.statement: For identical external scalars in a four-dimensional conformal field theory, the correlation function block is $g_{\Delta,\ell}=\frac{z\bar z}{z-\bar z}[k_{\Delta+\ell}(z)k_{\Delta-\ell-2}(\bar z)-k_{\Delta-\ell-2}(z)k_{\Delta+\ell}(\bar z)]$, with the hypergeometric $k$ of equation (168) and its OPE normalization.
hypotheses: The exchanged primary has dimension $\Delta$ and integer symmetric traceless spin $\ell$, and the external scalar dimensions agree. Identical scalars allow only even $\ell$ in the OPE. The spacetime dimension is exactly 4, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.

The parameters are regular, and a branch with the primary OPE asymptotics is chosen. The Casimir equation of the linked theorem applies with its own unitarity and projector assumptions. At $z=\bar z$ the block is the continuous extension of the quotient.

steps.text: Set $p=\Delta+\ell$ and $q=\Delta-\ell-2$, and $D_t=t^2(1-t)\partial_t^2-t^2\partial_t$. The two-dimensional result gives $D_tk_\beta=\tfrac\beta2(\tfrac\beta2-1)k_\beta$ for each $\beta$. So $f=k_p(z)k_q(\bar z)-k_q(z)k_p(\bar z)$ obeys $(D_z+D_{\bar z})f=\Lambda f$. Here $\Lambda=\tfrac p2(\tfrac p2-1)+\tfrac q2(\tfrac q2-1)$. Both terms of $f$ have this same sum. Expand: $\Lambda=\tfrac12[\Delta(\Delta-4)+\ell(\ell+2)]+2$.

Let $u=z\bar z/(z-\bar z)$ and $\delta=z-\bar z$. Let $E=(1-z)\partial_z-(1-\bar z)\partial_{\bar z}$. By equation (165) for $d=4$, the block obeys $Lg=\lambda g$ with $L=D_z+D_{\bar z}+2uE$ and $\lambda=\tfrac12[\Delta(\Delta-4)+\ell(\ell+2)]$. Put $g=uf$. We have $u_z=-\bar z^2/\delta^2$, $u_{\bar z}=z^2/\delta^2$, $u_{zz}=2\bar z^2/\delta^3$ and $u_{\bar z\bar z}=2z^2/\delta^3$. Terms with $f_z$: $D_z$ gives the mixed term $2z^2(1-z)u_zf_z=-2z^2\bar z^2(1-z)f_z/\delta^2$, and $2uE$ gives $2u^2(1-z)f_z=+2z^2\bar z^2(1-z)f_z/\delta^2$. They cancel. Terms with $f_{\bar z}$: $D_{\bar z}$ gives $+2z^2\bar z^2(1-\bar z)f_{\bar z}/\delta^2$, and $2uE$ gives the opposite. They cancel. Terms with $f$ alone: $D_zu=D_{\bar z}u=z^2\bar z^2(2-z-\bar z)/\delta^3$ and $Eu=-[\bar z^2(1-z)+z^2(1-\bar z)]/\delta^2$. The sum $D_zu+D_{\bar z}u+2uEu$ equals $2z\bar z\{z\bar z(2-z-\bar z)-(z^2+\bar z^2)+z\bar z(z+\bar z)\}/\delta^3=-2z\bar z\delta^2/\delta^3=-2u$. So $L(uf)=u(D_z+D_{\bar z}-2)f$. With s1 this is $u(\Lambda-2)f=\lambda\,uf$. Thus $g=uf$ has the eigenvalue $\lambda$ required by the cited Casimir theorem.

The small-$z,\bar z$ primary asymptotics fix the normalization in equation (167). Antisymmetry makes the numerator vanish at $z=\bar z$, so the apparent denominator singularity is removable at regular points. The source boundary condition takes z to zero first and then x to zero, with leading power $x^{\lambda_1}z^{\lambda_2}$. The regular primary branch and this leading coefficient determine the solution. The statement keeps the normalization of equation (167), which has no extra factor. A different convention for the block changes it only by a constant that depends on $\ell$.

applications.title: Remove the apparent diagonal singularity of a scalar block
applications.inputs: Take $\Delta=4$, $\ell=0$, so the parameters are $p=4,q=2$, and set $z,\bar z\to t=1/2$.
applications.hypotheses: Both hypergeometric factors are regular at $t=1/2$.

steps.text: Set $z=t+\epsilon$, $\bar z=t$. The antisymmetric numerator is $\epsilon[k_4'(t)k_2(t)-k_2'(t)k_4(t)]+O(\epsilon^2)$.
The prefactor tends to $t^2/\epsilon$. The product therefore tends to $t^2[k_4'(t)k_2(t)-k_2'(t)k_4(t)]$.

applications.conclusion: The block has a finite diagonal value, computed by a Wronskian rather than division by zero.

limitations: This is a result within the explicitly stated conformal field theory framework, not an existence theorem for an interacting model.

deferred.name: Radial Gegenbauer coefficients of unitary conformal blocks are nonnegative
deferred.statement: For identical real scalar pairs in a unitary conformal field theory with $d>2$, a conformal block in radial coordinates has correlation function expansion $g_{\Delta,\ell}=\sum_{n,j}B_{n,j}r^{\Delta+n}C_j^{(d-2)/2}(\cos\theta)$ with $B_{n,j}\geq0$ in the positive Gegenbauer normalization, for $r<1$.
hypotheses: The external pair is identical and real, and the radial representation is unitary. The Euclidean dimension is at least 2, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.

The two scalar pairs have radial separation $r<1$, and the descendant energy-spin basis is complete. Both identical pairs use opposite points at equal radius in the symmetric rho frame, and r is the absolute rho coordinate. The reduced function $g$ equals the pair-state matrix element of $r^D$ times a positive constant.

steps.text: Take the pair state $|\Psi_n\rangle=\phi(x)\phi(-x)|0\rangle$ with $x=n$ on the unit sphere, and let $P$ project on the conformal family of the exchanged primary. Define $G(r,n\cdot n')=\langle\Psi_{n'}|r^{D}P|\Psi_n\rangle$ with $r=e^{-\tau}$ and $D$ the dilatation. The reduced function $g_{\Delta,\ell}$ of the four-point block equals $c\,G$, where $c>0$ is the squared norm factor of the pair state. The powers of $r$ from the external dimensions cancel in the symmetric rho frame. So $g$ and $G$ differ only by the positive constant $c$, and positivity of $G$ gives positivity of $g$. A level-$n$ descendant has $D=\Delta+n$, so its term in $G$ contains $r^{\Delta+n}$ exactly.

The state $|\Psi_n\rangle$ is invariant under the $SO(d-1)$ that fixes the axis $n$. The level-$n$ space is a sum of $SO(d)$ irreps. An irrep has an $SO(d-1)$-invariant vector only if it is a symmetric traceless tensor of some spin $j$, and then this vector is unique (sphere harmonics: $L^2(S^{d-1})$ holds only these irreps, each once). So mixed-symmetry irreps give zero overlap. For spin $j$, the component of $|\Psi_n\rangle$ is $a\,|Z_n\rangle$, with $|Z_n\rangle$ the unit zonal vector and $a$ a complex number. Then $\langle Z_{n'}|Z_n\rangle=C_j^{(d-2)/2}(n\cdot n')/C_j^{(d-2)/2}(1)$ (the zonal function of spin $j$). Hence the spin-$j$ part of $G$ is $|a|^2/C_j^{(d-2)/2}(1)$ times $C_j^{(d-2)/2}(n\cdot n')$. The constant is positive.

Reality and radial adjoints make the remaining weight the sum of absolute squares of the overlap coefficients. Hence $B_{n,j}\geq0$. The identity of the two scalar insertions removes odd angular spin. At zero angle, positive Gegenbauer values also make each energy contribution nonnegative. In this symmetric frame, reversal of the axis exchanges the two identical insertions at the same radius and leaves the pair state fixed. An odd spherical harmonic changes sign under this reversal, so its overlap vanishes.

applications.title: Bound a truncation error at zero angle
applications.inputs: Suppose a unitary block in $d=3$ has known radial coefficients and take $\theta=0$, $r=1/4$.
applications.hypotheses: Use the positive Legendre normalization $C_j^{1/2}(1)=1$ and a convergent descendant sum.

steps.text: Every term is $B_{n,j}(1/4)^{\Delta+n}\geq0$.
A truncation through level 2 is therefore a lower bound on the exact block at this angle. The omitted sum is nonnegative.

applications.conclusion: At zero angle, truncation underestimates the block and the omitted radial terms cannot cancel.

limitations: This is a result within the explicitly stated conformal field theory framework, not an existence theorem for an interacting model.

deferred.name: A positive bootstrap functional excludes a proposed conformal spectrum
deferred.statement: In a unitary conformal field theory, write scalar crossing as $F_1+\sum_O p_OF_O=0$ with $p_O\geq0$. If a linear functional on these correlation function vectors obeys $\alpha(F_1)>0$, $\alpha(F_O)\geq0$ for every allowed exchange, and commutes with the convergent sum, the proposed spectrum is impossible.
hypotheses: The normalized identical-scalar block expansion is convergent, crossing holds, and its coefficients are nonnegative. The Euclidean dimension is at least 2, and the conformal covariance includes orthogonal reflections and inversion.
The functional is linear, preserves the convergent exchange sum, is positive on the identity, and is nonnegative on all allowed exchanges.

steps.text: Normalize the scalar two-point function to one, so its identity OPE coefficient is one. Let $g_O(u,v)$ be the block of the exchanged operator $O$ and $g_1=1$ the identity block. Crossing is the equality $v^{D}\sum_O p_O g_O(u,v)=u^{D}\sum_O p_O g_O(v,u)$, with $D$ the scalar dimension and the identity as $O=1$ with $p_1=1$. Move all terms to one side. Define the vectors $F_O=v^{D}g_O(u,v)-u^{D}g_O(v,u)$ for every $O$, including $F_1$ for the identity. Then crossing reads $F_1+\sum_{O\neq 1}p_OF_O=0$, with $p_O=f_{\phi\phi O}^2\geq0$.
Linearity and the stated interchange condition give $\alpha(F_1)+\sum_Op_O\alpha(F_O)=0$. Every term in the sum is nonnegative under the proposed spectrum.

The identity term is strictly positive. Adding the nonnegative exchange terms gives a strictly positive left side, which cannot equal zero. Thus no conformal data with that spectrum can obey both unitarity and crossing. A finite numerical sample alone does not establish positivity over the full allowed spectrum.

steps.text: Set $z=\bar z=t$ and let $t\downarrow0$. The identity contributes one. Every other global primary has positive dimension and its direct-channel block vanishes, so a finite proposed expansion tends to one.

A global factor $k_{2h}(1-t)$ is bounded by a constant times $1+|\log t|$ for regular positive $h$, from the zero-balanced hypergeometric equation. A weight-zero chiral factor is constant by its regular limit. Each two-dimensional global block is therefore at most of order $(1+|\log t|)^2$.

Crossing multiplies the crossed sum by $(t/(1-t))^{2\Delta_\phi}$. Since $\Delta_\phi>0$, this factor times any fixed logarithmic square tends to zero. A finite sum would make the same correlator tend both to zero and to one, a contradiction. The theorem counts global primaries, not Virasoro primaries.

steps.text: A finite set of global blocks would be multiplied in the crossed limit by $t^{1/4}$.
Even logarithmic-square growth cannot cancel this factor. Thus infinitely many global multiplets must occur, although only finitely many Virasoro families occur.

applications.conclusion: Finite Virasoro fusion rules do not imply a finite global-primary OPE.

deferred.name: The effective action sums one-particle irreducible vertices
deferred.statement: In finite-dimensional formal quantum field theory, the effective action is the quadratic action minus the exponential vertex series of amputated one-particle irreducible graph amplitudes. Its tree expansion reproduces the connected path integral generating function, including every loop correction of the original theory.
hypotheses: The free quadratic form is invertible and the interactions are formal symmetric tensors.

One-particle irreducibility means that the connected graph has no bridge between internal vertices, and automorphism weights include external labels. An external leg is not an internal edge. Amputation removes the free propagator from each external leg. The effective vertices carry the interaction vertex weights $1/n!$, and each loop carries one factor of $\hbar$. The grading is by the formal interaction parameters. The source $J$ is a linear source. Each source leg is a univalent vertex joined by an original propagator, and its edge is not counted as a bridge.

steps.text: Remove every edge whose removal disconnects the graph. Each remaining component has no bridge, and the graph formed by these components and the removed edges is a tree. A cycle in this skeleton would contradict the definition of a bridge.

Fix a number $n$ of external legs. Amputate each external leg: remove its free propagator and keep the leg as a label. Sum the amplitudes of all bridge-free connected graphs with $n$ amputated legs, each with weight $1/|\mathrm{Aut}|$ and with $\hbar^{L-1}$ for $L$ loops. These sums define the effective vertex tensors. They exclude the free propagator and the quadratic term. The original propagator contracts the internal bridge edges of the skeleton.

Let $W(J)$ be the connected generating function with source $J$. A source leg is a univalent vertex with weight $J$. Its edge is a bridge, and it joins the rest of the graph through an original propagator. Glue as follows. A connected graph $G$ with source legs splits uniquely into $m$ bridge-free components and trees of bridges (step 1). Component $i$ has $k_i$ legs. Label the components $1,\dots,m$ and the legs of component $i$ by $1,\dots,k_i$. Consider the labelled structures: such a tree wiring with such labels. The group $H=\prod_iS_{k_i}\rtimes S_m$ has order $m!\prod_ik_i!$ and relabels them. The stabilizer of a structure is $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$, which fixes the source legs. By orbit-stabilizer, the structures of $G$ number $m!\prod_ik_i!/|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|$. So $1/|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|=(\#\text{structures})/(m!\prod_ik_i!)$. Next fix a component type with $k$ legs. Let $K$ be the automorphisms that fix every leg. The sum over leg labellings of its isomorphism classes of $1/|K|$ equals $k!/|\mathrm{Aut}|$, since there are $k!/(|\mathrm{Aut}|/|K|)$ labellings and each has $|K|$ automorphisms. So the effective vertex $\Gamma_k=\frac1{k!}\sum_{\text{labelled}}A/|K|$ is the symmetric tensor with the $1/k!$ weight of the hypotheses. The tree series of $\Gamma$ sums over structures with the factor $1/m!$ from the exponential, and $1/k_i!$ from each $\Gamma_{k_i}$. Therefore each original graph $G$ appears once with weight $1/|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|$ and the same power of $\hbar$, because loops of $G$ are the loops of its components. Source legs contract with $J$ through the original propagator. The quadratic term of the effective action gives the free propagator on the two-point tree edge. So the tree series of the effective action with source $J$ equals $W(J)$.

deferred.name: The effective action is the Legendre transform of the connected generating function
deferred.statement: For a finite-dimensional formal quantum field theory with invertible free Hessian, let $W(J)=\hbar\log[Z(J)/Z_0]$ and $x=\partial_JW$. Its effective action is $\Gamma(x)=Jx-W(J)$ at the formal inverse $J(x)$. Thus $\partial_x\Gamma=J$, and $W$ is the inverse Legendre transform of $\Gamma$ for the path integral.
hypotheses: The source enters the action linearly as $-Jx$, and the connected generator has invertible Hessian at the expansion point.

The effective action $\Gamma$ is the one-particle irreducible effective action of the linked theorem, taken with the sign convention $\Gamma=S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ so that the tree relation $W(J)=Jx-\Gamma(x)$ holds. The same vacuum normalization is used.

steps.text: A source is a one-valent vertex of the connected graphs that give $W(J)$. In a one-particle irreducible amputated graph, an external leg is not an internal edge, and a source vertex would have its single incident edge as a bridge. So no such graph contains a source. Thus the vertex tensors of $\Gamma$ do not depend on $J$, and $\Gamma$ is a function of $x$ alone. The source $J$ enters only through the tree expansion of $W$, as the stationarity condition $\partial_x\Gamma(x)=J$.

The effective tree theorem gives $W(J)=Jx_0-\Gamma(x_0)$ where $\partial_x\Gamma(x_0)=J$. The invertible free Hessian makes this stationary point a well-defined formal series in $J$ and the interactions.

Differentiate with respect to $J$. The terms containing $\partial_Jx_0$ cancel by stationarity, so $\partial_JW=x_0$. Solving for $J(x)$ yields $\Gamma(x)=J(x)x-W(J(x))$. Its derivative is $J$, which proves both Legendre relations.

applications.title: Recover the effective action of a free Gaussian
applications.inputs: Take a free one-variable theory with Hessian $a>0$ and linear source $J$.
applications.hypotheses: The Gaussian generator has invertible second derivative and the reference vacuum normalization is fixed.

steps.text: Completing the square gives $W(J)=J^2/(2a)$, so $x=J/a$ and $J=ax$.
Then $\Gamma(x)=ax^2-a^2x^2/(2a)=ax^2/2$.

applications.conclusion: The Legendre transform recovers the free quadratic effective action.

proof.verification: Cited published proof outline; no formal check.
proof.scope: Outline of the published proof. Derivation of the stated value from three cited inputs: Mumford's cell-model theorem, Quillen's Euler characteristic formula, and the Stirling series for $\Gamma'/\Gamma$. The steps show the arc-system count, the gluing relations and the series evaluation.

steps.text: Mumford's theorem (cited) gives a contractible complex $Y_g$ with a cellular action of the pointed mapping class group. The action has finitely many cell orbits and finite stabilizers. A filling arc system with $n$ arcs gives a cell of dimension $6g-3-n$. Quillen's formula gives $\chi=\sum_\sigma(-1)^{\dim\sigma}/|\mathrm{Stab}\,\sigma|$, so the sign of a cell is $(-1)^{n-1}$. The dual of a filling system has one 2-cell. This 2-cell is a $2n$-gon with sides glued in pairs to a surface of genus $g$. Each system arises from $2n/|\mathrm{Stab}\,\sigma|$ labelled gluings. Arcs are not null-homotopic exactly when no side is glued to a neighbour (A). Arcs are not homotopic to each other exactly when no two consecutive sides are glued to two consecutive sides in opposite order (B). Let $\lambda_g(n)$ count the gluings that satisfy (A) and (B). Then $\chi=\sum_{n\geq1}(-1)^{n-1}\lambda_g(n)/(2n)$.

Let $\varepsilon_g(n)$ and $\mu_g(n)$ count gluings of a labelled $2n$-gon with no condition and with only (A). Glue neighbouring glued sides until none are left. This gives a $(2n-2i)$-gon that satisfies (A). The $i$ new interior vertices have smallest labels that form an $i$-subset of $\{1,\dots,2n\}$, and this subset recovers the gluing. So $\varepsilon_g(n)=\sum_i\binom{2n}{i}\mu_g(n-i)$. In the same way, merge consecutive sides glued in opposite order. The merge data sum to $i$ and the count of ways to label is $\binom{n}{i}$. So $\mu_g(n)=\sum_i\binom{n}{i}\lambda_g(n-i)$. The Harer-Zagier moment formula gives $P_n(x)=\sum_g\varepsilon_g(n)x^{n+1-2g}=\frac{(2n)!}{2^n n!}\sum_p\binom np 2^p\binom{x}{p+1}$. Put $q=n-p$. Only terms with $q\leq2g$ give $x^{-2g}$ in $P_n(x)/x^{n+1}$. The Stirling expansion of $Q(x,a)=\Gamma(x)/(\Gamma(x-a)x^a)$ has coefficients that are polynomials in $a$. Also $Q(x,-1)=1$ and $Q(x,0)=1$. Hence $\varepsilon_g(n)=\binom{2n}{n}f_g(n)$ with $f_g$ a polynomial and $f_g(0)=0$.

Let $E,M,L$ be the generating series of $\varepsilon,\mu,\lambda$. The two relations give $E(z)=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4z}}{2(1-4z)}\,L\!\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4z}}{2\sqrt{1-4z}}\right)$. Test this on $P(z)=(1+a)z-1$ and integrate with an Euler Beta integral. The result is $\sum_{n\geq1}(-1)^{n-1}\lambda(n)/(2n)=f'(0)$ for every polynomial $f$ with $f(0)=0$. So $\chi=f_g'(0)$. Terms with $q>1$ are divisible by $n^2$, so they do not change $f_g'(0)$. The terms $q=1$ and $q=0$ give $\sum_g f_g'(0)x^{-2g}=\frac1{2x}+\frac{\Gamma'(x)}{\Gamma(x)}-\log x$. The asymptotic series $\Gamma'/\Gamma\sim\log x-\frac1{2x}-\sum_g\frac{B_{2g}}{2g\,x^{2g}}$ (cited) gives $f_g'(0)=-B_{2g}/(2g)$. Hence $\chi(\mathcal M_{g,1})=-B_{2g}/(2g)$.

source.ref: P. Etingof, Mathematical Ideas and Notions of Quantum Field Theory, MIT 18.238 lecture notes (2023). Section 5.3, Theorem 5.4; Sections 5.4-5.7, pp. 67-76.

The finite-mode coherent-state calculation identifies a periodic Grassmann time boundary with a trace containing $(-1)^F$. Time-ordered insertions remain inside this trace. Antiperiodic sewing would instead give the ordinary trace.

The source free propagator is the inverse of the periodic first-order kinetic operator. The Fock supertrace has the same two-point contraction, and the fermionic Wick theorem fixes every higher product. The denominator factorizes as $\prod_j(e^{Lm_j}-e^{-Lm_j})$, which is nonzero for positive L and nonzero masses.

applications.title: Compute a one-mode periodic fermion partition function
applications.inputs: Take one complex mode with $m=1$ and circle length $L=1$.
applications.hypotheses: The mass is nonzero and the boundary condition is periodic.

steps.text: The empty mode has energy -1 and even parity. The occupied mode has energy +1 and odd parity.
The supertrace is therefore $e^1-e^{-1}=2\sinh1$. The ordinary antiperiodic thermal partition function would be $e^1+e^{-1}$.

applications.conclusion: The periodic fermion partition function is $2\sinh1$.
